thesis: C3.ai, Inc. (NYSE: AI) sells enterprise application software for artificial intelligence: a model-driven platform used to build, deploy, and operate predictive and generative AI applications for large organizations. **[Fact]** The company reports as a single operating segment. **[Fact]** FY2026 revenue (year ended April 30, 2026) was **$227.1 million**, down from **$327.6 million** in FY2025 per XBRL-tagged filing extracts in `filing_facts_2026-08-06.json`. **[Fact]** Cash and cash equivalents were **$66.2 million** with **no reported long-term debt** at the April 30, 2026 balance sheet date on the FY2026 10-K. **[Inference]** C3.ai is an application-layer enterprise AI vendor competing with hyperscaler platforms and specialized software peers; owner economics today depend on converting large-deal pipeline into durable subscription revenue without further dilution.
why_market_wrong: The market may overweight **CEO Thomas Siebel's return**, **Federal and Shell partnership headlines**, and **episodic insider purchases** while underweighting a **31% revenue decline**, an **unproven switching-cost moat** against hyperscalers, and **stock-based compensation dilution**. **[Inference]** At about **$11.34** (Yahoo close 2026-10-08 in `valuation.json`), the stock still embeds recovery in normalized owner cash that filings have not confirmed: our base case uses **$0.80 per share** starting owner cash **[Assumption]**, not spot GAAP earnings (mechanical net income tags in the filing extract conflict with loss-making history and are not used as the cash anchor). **[Inference]** The universal contract sums four non-overlapping components to roughly **$21 per share** base intrinsic value at the prior price stub; at a higher spot price, implied contract returns compress even if pipeline optionality is real. Moat durability remains the binding gate.
